blocks.text: In 1928 the British biologist Frederick Griffith worked with the pathogenic bacterium Streptococcus pneumoniae, which has two strains. The S-type strain has a polysaccharide coat and forms smooth colonies; the R-type strain lacks the coat and forms rough colonies.

blocks.alt: Four columns, each a dish of bacteria injected into a mouse. Live S cells with capsules: the mouse dies. Live R cells without capsules: the mouse lives. Heat-killed S cells: the mouse lives. Heat-killed S cells mixed with live R cells: the mouse dies and live S cells are found in its blood.
blocks.caption: Griffith's four injections (original diagram after Figure 19.6).
blocks.long_description: In 1928 Griffith worked with Streptococcus pneumoniae. The S strain has a polysaccharide coat and smooth colonies and is virulent; the R strain lacks the coat, forms rough colonies and is harmless. Live S cells killed mice, live R cells and heat-killed S cells did not, but a mixture of heat-killed S and live R cells killed the mice, and live S bacteria were recovered from their blood. Something from the dead S cells had changed the R cells into virulent, coated S cells; Griffith called this transformation, but he could not tell whether the transforming material was DNA, protein or both.

items: Live S-type bacteria injected into mice were virulent (lethal): the mice developed pneumonia and died.
Live R-type bacteria had no effect on the mice.
Heat-killed S-type bacteria left the mice healthy, so Griffith thought the virulence might come from the polysaccharide coat that protects S cells from the host's immune system.
A mixture of heat-killed S-type and live R-type bacteria, expected to be harmless, killed the mice, and many live S-type bacteria were found in their blood.

blocks.title: Transformation
blocks.text: Griffith concluded that the information for making the polysaccharide coat and virulence passed from the heat-killed S-type to the live R-type bacteria, which made the coat and became virulent S-type. He called this transformation: the transfer of genetic material from one organism to another, changing the genetic makeup of the recipient. He could not find whether the transferred material was DNA, protein or both.

blocks.title: Information: Avery, MacLeod and McCarty (1944)
blocks.text: These three scientists identified the transforming principle. When proteins were removed from dead S-type bacteria and the rest mixed with live R-type, the injected mice still became diseased and live S-type bacteria were found, so proteins were not responsible. When all DNA was removed from dead S-type before mixing with live R-type, no transformation occurred and the mice stayed healthy. They concluded that DNA is the transforming principle.
